notes.front: What is the FAA, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Federal Aviation Administration: the US government agency that sets safety standards for civil aviation.
notes.explanation: Its rules sit in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR), and they are the rules this deck teaches.
notes.example: Like a road authority that both licenses drivers and sets car-safety standards: FAA rules cover everything from earning a pilot certificate to maintaining an aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 1, “The Role of the FAA”, p. 1-7

notes.front: In FAA regulations, what is an aircraft, in one sentence?
notes.back: A device that is used or intended to be used for flight in the air.
notes.explanation: It is the widest term in the rules. An unmanned aircraft is defined as a kind of aircraft, so in law a drone is an aircraft.
notes.example: An airliner, a helicopter and a small camera drone are all aircraft: each is a device used for flight in the air.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions, "Aircraft" (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is an unmanned aircraft, in one sentence?
notes.back: An aircraft operated without the possibility of direct human intervention from within or on the aircraft.
notes.explanation: What makes it unmanned is that nobody on board can intervene; control comes from outside the aircraft. The AIM abbreviates unmanned aircraft as UA.
notes.example: A quadcopter flown from a hand-held controller is an unmanned aircraft; a light aeroplane with a pilot in the seat is not.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR); AIM para. 7-6-6 (abbreviation UA)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is a small unmanned aircraft, in one sentence?
notes.back: An unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything on board or attached to it.
notes.explanation: The weight includes the payload, so a camera, sprayer tank or parcel counts toward the limit. The FAA’s Remote Pilot Study Guide calls it a “small UA”.
notes.example: A 40 lb drone carrying a 10 lb sprayer tank weighs 50 lb on takeoff, so it is still a small unmanned aircraft.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR); Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (term “small UA”)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is a small unmanned aircraft system (small UAS), in one sentence?
notes.back: A small unmanned aircraft plus the elements needed to fly it safely, including communication links and the components that control it.
notes.explanation: The rules often regulate the whole system, not just the airframe: the controller and the radio link are part of it.
notes.example: A drone, its hand-held controller and the radio link between them together form one small UAS.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is part 107, in one sentence?
notes.back: The FAA rule (14 CFR part 107) covering registration, pilot certification and operation of civil small UAS in the United States.
notes.explanation: It is the rule this whole deck teaches. Since 2021 it also decides which small UAS may fly over people.
notes.example: A roofer who flies a drone to photograph a roof for a customer is flying under part 107.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.1 Applicability (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is a control station, in one sentence?
notes.back: An interface used to control the flight path of the small unmanned aircraft.
notes.explanation: The definition is about function, not hardware: whatever interface commands the flight path is the control station.
notes.example: A hand-held radio controller, or a tablet app that sends the drone its route, each serves as a control station.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is a remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating, in one sentence?
notes.back: The FAA certificate a person must hold to act as the pilot in command of a small UAS under part 107.
notes.explanation: In aviation the FAA calls licensing "certification". Earning this certificate is the goal of the exam this deck prepares for.
notes.example: Like a driving licence, but for being the pilot in command of a small drone under part 107.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶6.1–6.2; 14 CFR § 107.12(b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: What is the remote pilot in command (remote PIC), in one sentence?
notes.back: The person who holds a remote pilot certificate and has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the flight.
notes.explanation: Whoever is actually holding the controls, the remote PIC answers for the flight. One must be designated before or during each flight.
notes.example: A survey firm's certificated pilot is remote PIC while a trainee flies the drone beside her; she stays responsible.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.2.7; 14 CFR § 107.19
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: Who is the "person manipulating the controls", in one sentence?
notes.back: Someone other than the remote PIC who is flying the small unmanned aircraft under the remote PIC's supervision.
notes.explanation: Part 107 lets a person without a certificate fly, but only in this supervised arrangement.
notes.example: A client tries the controls during a job while the certificated remote PIC stands ready to take over.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.2.6
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: What is a visual observer (VO), in one sentence?
notes.back: A person the remote PIC designates to help see and avoid other air traffic or objects in the air or on the ground.
notes.explanation: The visual observer is an extra pair of eyes for the remote PIC and the person manipulating the controls; part 107 treats one as optional ("if a visual observer is used").
notes.example: During a roof inspection, a colleague watches the sky for helicopters and calls them out to the pilot.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR); § 107.33
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is a direct participant in a small UAS operation, in one sentence?
notes.back: A person whose involvement is necessary for the safe operation of the small UAS.
notes.explanation: The remote PIC, the person manipulating the controls and a visual observer are the usual direct participants; bystanders are not.
notes.example: At a film shoot, the visual observer is a direct participant; a passer-by walking a dog is not.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: In part 107, what are corrective lenses?
notes.back: Spectacles or contact lenses.
notes.explanation: The term matters for keeping the drone in sight: the rule allows vision aided by corrective lenses but by no other device.
notes.example: Flying in your prescription glasses is flying with corrective lenses; watching through binoculars is not.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR); § 107.31(a)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: In drone law, what is a community-based organization (CBO)?
notes.back: The kind of organization whose set of safety guidelines, developed in coordination with the FAA, recreational drone flyers follow.
notes.explanation: Flying within a CBO’s safety guidelines is one of the conditions, set out on the next card, for flying purely for fun without a remote pilot certificate.
notes.example: Like a sports club’s safety code: a hobby flyer follows the CBO’s guidelines, while a paid photographer follows part 107.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ch. 4, footnote 1 (49 U.S.C. 44809(a)), p. 4-6

notes.front: What is recreational flying under 49 U.S.C. 44809, in one sentence?
notes.back: Flying a small unmanned aircraft strictly for recreation within limits set by statute, without FAA certification or operating authority.
notes.explanation: It sits outside part 107: a hobby flyer who keeps to every 44809 limit needs no remote pilot certificate.
notes.example: Flying for fun in a park under a community-based organization's safety guidelines is 44809 flying; filming the park for a paying client is not.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.1, footnote 1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: As 14 CFR § 3.5 defines it, what does "airworthy" mean?
notes.back: The aircraft conforms to its type design (the design the FAA approved for that model) and is in a condition for safe operation.
notes.explanation: Most part 107 drones carry no airworthiness certificate, but the idea appears in part 107's exclusions and in the rules for certificated drones.
notes.example: A drone built exactly to its approved design and undamaged is airworthy; the same drone with a cracked arm is not in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 3.5(a) Definitions, "Airworthy" (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 3 as of that date

notes.front: What are the operations-over-people categories in part 107, in one sentence?
notes.back: Four categories (1 to 4) in part 107 subpart D, each setting how a small UAS may qualify to fly over people.
notes.explanation: A remote PIC may fly over people only in line with one of these categories (or a narrow exception); the deck teaches each category later.
notes.example: A drone listed on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance for Category 2, and labelled "Category 2", may fly Category 2 operations over people.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.105 Limitations on operations over human beings (eCFR); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶8.11.2.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is a declaration of compliance, in one sentence?
notes.back: A record submitted to the FAA certifying that a small unmanned aircraft meets the Category 2 or Category 3 requirements.
notes.explanation: It is how a maker shows a model qualifies for flight over people. Part 89 uses a similar declaration for remote identification equipment.
notes.example: A manufacturer declares that serial numbers 1000 to 1999 of its model meet the Category 2 requirements.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR); § 107.160(a); 14 CFR § 89.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: In FAA rules, what is falsification, in one sentence?
notes.back: Making a fraudulent or intentionally false statement, or a fraudulent reproduction or alteration, in a document given to or kept for the FAA.
notes.explanation: The FAA relies on what owners and remote pilots tell it when it authorises flights or checks compliance, so false records undermine everything.
notes.example: Editing the date on a knowledge test report so it looks recent would be a fraudulent alteration.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 3.403 Falsification, reproduction, alteration, or omission (eCFR); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.3
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 3 as of that date

notes.front: For part 107 reporting, what counts as a serious injury, in one sentence?
notes.back: An injury at Level 3 or higher on the Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS).
notes.explanation: The AIS ranks injury severity and is widely used by emergency medical staff; the FAA uses AIS Level 3 as its threshold in other rules too.
notes.example: The AC's AIS 3 example: a person is admitted to hospital but can fully heal, such as a broken bone or a cut that needs stitches.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.4
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: What is a part 107 safety event report, in one sentence?
notes.back: A report due after serious injury, loss of consciousness, or other property damage unless repair (or, if destroyed, its value) is $500 or less.
notes.explanation: The remote PIC sends it to the FAA. Part 107 used to call it accident reporting; § 107.9 was retitled "Safety event reporting" in December 2022.
notes.example: A drone falls and cracks a car windscreen that costs $900 to replace: the remote PIC must report it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: In FAA rules, what is an exemption?
notes.back: Permission from the FAA to do something a rule otherwise forbids, asked for by petition under 14 CFR part 11.
notes.explanation: Part 107 does not apply to an operation that an exemption holder chooses to conduct under that exemption (§107.1(b)(3)).
notes.example: Part 107 bans carrying hazardous materials on a small drone; an operator may carry them only if it holds an exemption that permits it.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.15.2, p. 5-13; 14 CFR § 107.1(b)(3); 14 CFR part 11 (petitions for exemption)

notes.front: What is the NTSB, in one sentence?
notes.back: The National Transportation Safety Board: a federal board whose rules (49 CFR part 830) require immediate notification of certain aircraft accidents.
notes.explanation: It is separate from the FAA, so some drone accidents must be notified to the NTSB as well as reported to the FAA.
notes.example: If someone dies in a drone accident, the NTSB must be notified immediately, on top of the report to the FAA.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.4.2, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Reporting, p. 4-7

notes.front: What is the TSA, and why does it matter to a remote pilot applicant?
notes.back: The Transportation Security Administration: it security-vets every applicant before a remote pilot certificate is issued.
notes.explanation: After the FAA receives an application, the TSA vets the applicant; if vetting fails, no certificate is issued.
notes.example: An applicant who fails the TSA’s security threat assessment gets no certificate, and may appeal the decision to the TSA.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶6.5, Security Disqualification, p. 6-4

notes.front: Which aircraft and activities does part 107 apply to?
notes.back: The registration, pilot certification and operation of civil small UAS within the United States.
notes.explanation: It also governs whether a civil small UAS is eligible to fly over people. "Civil" means not government ("public") aircraft, such as police or military flights: AC 107-2A lists public aircraft operations as outside part 107.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.1 Applicability (eCFR), (a); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Part 107 does not apply to {{c1::air carrier}} operations.
notes.explanation: It is one of four exclusions in § 107.1(b). The others: 44809 recreational aircraft, flights under an exemption, and airworthiness-certificated drones flown under part 91.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.1 Applicability (eCFR), (b)(1)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Does part 107 apply to recreational flying (44809)?
notes.back: No. Aircraft subject to 49 U.S.C. 44809 are excluded from part 107.
notes.explanation: A recreational flyer who meets the 44809 limits follows those limits instead of part 107.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.1 Applicability (eCFR), (b)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A company holds an FAA exemption under 49 U.S.C. 44807 and chooses to fly a job under that exemption. Does part 107 apply to that flight?
notes.back: No, unless the exemption itself says otherwise.
notes.explanation: Part 107 excludes operations a holder of an exemption under 49 U.S.C. 44807 (or the older section 333 of Public Law 112-95) elects to conduct under the exemption.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.1 Applicability (eCFR), (b)(3)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: When may a small UAS that has an airworthiness certificate be flown outside part 107?
notes.back: When the operator elects to fly it under part 91 (the FAA's general operating and flight rules) instead.
notes.explanation: Part 107 does not apply to part 91 operations of a small UAS that has been issued an airworthiness certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.1 Applicability (eCFR), (b)(4)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: According to AC 107-2A, does part 107 apply to kites, moored balloons or amateur rockets?
notes.back: No. The AC also lists unmanned free balloons, public aircraft operations and operations outside the United States as outside part 107.
notes.explanation: Part 107 is about civil small UAS in the United States; these other things have their own rules.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: When do the part 21 certification procedures for products apply to a small UAS flown under part 107?
notes.back: Only if it will fly over people as a Category 4 operation.
notes.explanation: Otherwise, small UAS operated under part 107 are outside part 21, the FAA's rules for certificating aircraft and parts.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.2 Applicability of certification procedures for products and articles (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A small unmanned aircraft weighs less than {{c1::55 pounds}} on takeoff, counting everything on board or attached.
notes.explanation: Heavier unmanned aircraft are not small unmanned aircraft, so part 107 does not cover them.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A 48 lb crop-spraying drone takes off carrying 9 lb of liquid. Is it a small unmanned aircraft?
notes.back: No. It weighs 57 lb on takeoff, over the limit (less than 55 lb), so part 107 does not cover it.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: only the airframe's 48 lb counts
B) No: 57 lb on takeoff is over the limit
C) Yes: payloads are exempt from the weight limit
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the weight is measured on takeoff and includes everything on board or otherwise attached.
notes.explanation: The takeoff weight includes everything on board or attached, so the liquid counts.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Besides the aircraft itself, what does a small UAS include?
notes.back: The communication links and control components required for its safe and efficient operation.
notes.explanation: So a failed controller or radio link is a problem with the small UAS, not just with a piece of kit.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Is the radio link between a drone and its controller part of the small UAS, or separate from it?
notes.back: Part of the small UAS.
notes.explanation: The small UAS is the aircraft plus its associated elements, including communication links and control components.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Who is directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of a small UAS?
notes.back: The remote PIC.
notes.explanation: This mirrors a manned aircraft's pilot in command, whose authority is also final.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.19 Remote pilot in command (eCFR), (b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A remote PIC must be designated {{c1::before or during}} the flight.
notes.explanation: Remote PIC status can also pass between certificated pilots mid-flight, by positively communicating the transfer of control.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.19 Remote pilot in command (eCFR), (a); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.2.1.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A certificated pilot lets a colleague without a certificate fly the drone under her supervision. Who has final authority over the flight?
notes.back: The certificated pilot, as remote PIC; the colleague is the person manipulating the controls.
notes.explanation: Handing over the controls does not hand over responsibility; the remote PIC keeps final authority.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.2.6–4.2.7; 14 CFR § 107.19(b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: Who designates a visual observer?
notes.back: The remote PIC.
notes.explanation: The visual observer assists both the remote PIC and the person manipulating the controls to see and avoid.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: On a bridge inspection, a crew member picked by the remote PIC watches the sky and calls out an approaching helicopter. What role is she playing?
notes.back: Visual observer.
notes.explanation: A visual observer is designated by the remote PIC to help see and avoid other air traffic or objects.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: At a filming site, which of these is a direct participant: the visual observer, a spectator filming on a phone, or a passing cyclist?
notes.back: The visual observer.
notes.explanation: A direct participant is someone whose involvement is necessary for safe operation; the spectator and the cyclist are not involved in it.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: For recreational flying (44809), what purpose must the flight be for?
notes.back: Strictly recreational purposes.
notes.explanation: It is the first of eight statutory conditions; the flight must also follow a community-based organization's safety guidelines developed with the FAA.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.1, footnote 1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: For recreational flying (44809), what test must the flyer pass?
notes.back: An aeronautical knowledge and safety test, keeping proof of passing to show the FAA or law enforcement on request.
notes.explanation: The recreational test is not the remote pilot certificate; it does not allow part 107 flying.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.1, footnote 1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: A hobbyist who flies under the 44809 rules is paid by a neighbour to photograph her garden. Can that flight be recreational flying (44809)?
notes.back: No. 44809 flights must be strictly recreational, so a paid job falls under part 107.
notes.explanation: Once a flight is not strictly recreational, the 44809 exclusion no longer applies and part 107 does.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.1, footnote 1; 14 CFR § 107.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: Where is the FAA's rule against falsification now found, since § 107.5 is "[Reserved]"?
notes.back: 14 CFR § 3.403, in part 3, subpart D.
notes.explanation: Older study material (and AC 107-2A) still cites § 107.5; the current eCFR shows it reserved and the rule in part 3.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.5 [Reserved] and § 3.403 (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 3 as of that date

notes.front: What can falsification lead to?
notes.back: Denial, suspension, modification or revocation of certificates and other approvals, or a civil penalty.
notes.explanation: The same consequences apply to fraudulent reproduction or alteration and to knowingly omitting a material fact.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 3.403(d) (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 3 as of that date

notes.front: Besides fraudulent or intentionally false statements, what two other acts does § 3.403 prohibit?
notes.back: Producing, reproducing or altering documents for a fraudulent purpose, and knowingly omitting a material fact.
notes.explanation: It covers any document in any format submitted to the FAA or kept to show compliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 3 as of that date

notes.front: On an application to the FAA, a remote pilot knowingly leaves out a material fact that would count against him. What rule applies, and what can follow?
notes.back: The falsification rule (§ 3.403) on knowing omission; it can lead to denial or revocation, or a civil penalty.
notes.explanation: Knowingly omitting a material fact is prohibited just like a false statement.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 3 as of that date

notes.front: What must you have with you when exercising the privileges of your remote pilot certificate?
notes.back: The certificate and identification, in your physical possession and readily accessible.
notes.explanation: This applies to the remote PIC, the owner or the person manipulating the controls.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.7 Inspection, testing, and demonstration of compliance (eCFR), (a)(1)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What three details must the identification you present with your remote pilot certificate show?
notes.back: Your photograph, signature and date of birth.
notes.explanation: § 107.7 points to the knowledge-test identification rule, § 107.67(b)(1) to (3).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.7 Inspection, testing, and demonstration of compliance (eCFR), (a)(2); § 107.67(b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Besides law enforcement officers, which three bodies may ask to inspect your remote pilot certificate?
notes.back: The FAA, the National Transportation Safety Board and the Transportation Security Administration.
notes.explanation: Any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer may ask as well.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.7 Inspection, testing, and demonstration of compliance (eCFR), (a)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Mid-job, a county sheriff's deputy asks to see your remote pilot certificate. Must you show it?
notes.back: Yes, with your identification: any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer may ask.
notes.explanation: The certificate must be in your physical possession and readily accessible, so you can show it on the spot.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.7 Inspection, testing, and demonstration of compliance (eCFR), (a)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: On request, what may the FAA test or inspect to check compliance with part 107?
notes.back: The small UAS and the people operating it: remote PIC, person manipulating the controls and any visual observer.
notes.explanation: Those people, and the owner or operator, must allow the test or inspection.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.7 Inspection, testing, and demonstration of compliance (eCFR), (b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: On request, what must a holder of an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance let the FAA do?
notes.back: Inspect its facilities, technical data and any manufactured small UAS, and witness tests needed to check compliance.
notes.explanation: It must also make the declaration and any required records available on request.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.7 Inspection, testing, and demonstration of compliance (eCFR), (c)–(d)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A reportable safety event must be reported to the FAA no later than {{c1::10 calendar days}} after the operation.
notes.explanation: The duty falls on the remote PIC. It is separate from any report the FAA requests after an in-flight emergency.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Which harm to people makes a small UAS flight reportable?
notes.back: Serious injury to any person, or any loss of consciousness.
notes.explanation: Loss of consciousness is reportable even if the injury is not serious.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR), (a)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: When is damage to property not reportable?
notes.back: When repair costs $500 or less, or, if the property is a total loss, its fair market value is $500 or less.
notes.explanation: Repair cost includes materials and labour. Either condition exempts the damage from reporting.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR), (b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Does damage to the small unmanned aircraft itself count toward the $500 threshold?
notes.back: No. Only damage to property other than the small unmanned aircraft counts.
notes.explanation: Crashing and destroying your own drone, with no other harm, is not a reportable safety event.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR), (b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Your drone hits a parked car and the dent costs $750 to repair. Nobody is hurt. Must you report it?
notes.back: Yes, to the FAA within 10 calendar days: repair costs over $500.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, within 10 calendar days
B) No, because nobody was hurt
C) Only if the FAA asks
notes.choicesExplained: B: property damage alone is reportable above $500. C: the report is required regardless of any FAA request.
notes.explanation: Only if the repair cost ($750 here) were $500 or less would the damage be exempt.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Your drone destroys a garden ornament with a fair market value of $200. Must you report it?
notes.back: No: the property is a total loss worth $500 or less.
notes.explanation: For a total loss, the test is the property's fair market value, not the cost of a new one.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR), (b)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Your drone causes $200 of damage to a fence worth $600. Must you report it?
notes.back: No: the repair costs $500 or less.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A gives this same kind of example; what matters is the $200 repair, not the fence's value.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR), (b)(1); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.4
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Your $1,500 drone is destroyed in a crash on empty farmland. Nobody is hurt and nothing else is damaged. Must you report it?
notes.back: No: damage to the small unmanned aircraft itself does not count.
notes.explanation: Only serious injury, loss of consciousness, or damage to any property other than the drone itself (above the $500 test) triggers a report.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR), (b)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A falling drone strikes a spectator, who blacks out briefly but needs no hospital care. Must you report it?
notes.back: Yes: any loss of consciousness is reportable, within 10 calendar days.
notes.explanation: The injury need not be serious; loss of consciousness alone meets the threshold.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.9 Safety event reporting (eCFR), (a)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A person hit by a drone is admitted to hospital for a cut that must be stitched, and will fully heal. Is this a serious injury?
notes.back: Yes: it is an AIS Level 3 injury, so it is reportable.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A's AIS 3 example is a person who requires hospitalization for injuries such as broken bones or cuts needing stitches.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.4
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: How can a part 107 safety event report be submitted?
notes.back: Online at faa.gov/uas, or by phone to an FAA Regional Operations Center; Flight Standards offices also accept reports.
notes.explanation: The report should include the pilot's details and certificate number, the registration number, where and when it happened, and what happened.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.4.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: When must an unmanned aircraft accident also be notified to the National Transportation Safety Board?
notes.back: When anyone dies or is seriously injured, or an aircraft of 300 lb or more maximum gross takeoff weight is substantially damaged.
notes.explanation: The NTSB requires immediate notification, in addition to the FAA report; its own rules (49 CFR part 830) define the terms.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.4.2
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: How long must someone who declared compliance and produces the aircraft keep the supporting data?
notes.back: Two years after production of that small UAS ends.
notes.explanation: They must make it available to the FAA on request.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.165 Record retention (eCFR), (a)(2)(i)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: How long must someone who declared compliance for a small unmanned aircraft they designed or modified keep the supporting data?
notes.back: Two years after they submitted the declaration of compliance.
notes.explanation: Contrast producers, whose two years run from the end of production.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.165 Record retention (eCFR), (a)(2)(ii)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Your drone was made before the operations-over-people rules and carries no category label. Before flying it over people as Category 2, what must you do?
notes.back: Check whether it is listed on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance and, if it is eligible, label it yourself.
notes.explanation: An aircraft without a clear, legible category label is not eligible to fly over people; the remote pilot is responsible for the label.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶8.11.2.3
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: When may one small UAS be eligible for more than one operations-over-people category?
notes.back: When the remote PIC cannot inadvertently switch between its modes or configurations.
notes.explanation: A drone might, for example, meet one category in one configuration and another in a second; accidental switching must be impossible.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.150 Variable mode and variable configuration of small unmanned aircraft systems (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is the difference between a small unmanned aircraft and a small UAS?
notes.back: The small unmanned aircraft is the aircraft itself (under 55 lb); the small UAS adds its communication links and control components.
notes.explanation: Rules about weight speak of the aircraft; rules about the whole operation often speak of the system.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.3 Definitions (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What is the difference between the remote PIC and the person manipulating the controls?
notes.back: The remote PIC holds the certificate and final authority; the person manipulating the controls flies under the remote PIC's supervision.
notes.explanation: They can be the same person; when they are not, responsibility stays with the remote PIC.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.2.6–4.2.7
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: How does the FAA's 10-day safety event report differ from NTSB notification?
notes.back: The FAA report is due within 10 calendar days; the NTSB requires immediate notification, and only for events meeting its own accident definition.
notes.explanation: A single event can require both: for example, a death. The NTSB uses its own definitions of "serious injury" and "substantial damage" (49 CFR 830.2).
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶4.4–4.4.2
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date
